newsitem.title: BELGIUM: TV channels take subsidy row to political arena.
newsitem.headline: TV channels take subsidy row to political arena.

text.p: A group of EU states, concerned that the European Commission may try to clamp down on subsidies to public television broadcasters, is proposing to exclude the sector altogether from competition rules.

The proposal for a protocol attached to the new EU treaty expected to be signed in Amsterdam in June came from Belgium, but it was initiated by the Netherlands -- which currently holds the EU presidency, EU and industry sources said.
The idea is opposed by commercial TV channels which have been crying foul in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal over their rivals receiving public funding while competing for advertising revenue.

"The proposed protocol questions the competence of the Commission and the Court of Justice to justify the non- application of competition rules and goes against the basis of the internal market rules by pushing for the renationalisation of an entire services sector," Jan Mojto, managing director of the German media group Kirch, said in a statement.
Mojto is also president of the Association of Commercial Television in Europe (ACT).
The Belgian proposal received immediate support from Sweden, Portugal, Germany, Italy and Greece, a diplomat said.
France, Austria, Finland, Ireland and Luxembourg are also concerned that the Commission may try to put some order into public money handed to public broadcasters, he said.

Even Britain, supported by the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), seems to be in favour of some "clarification" of national governments' right to fund state-controlled channels, another diplomat said.
To be adopted the draft protocal requires the unanimous consent of all EU states.

The Commission last year rejected a challenge by television company Sociedade Independente de Communicacao (SIC) of media tycoon and former Portuguese Prime Minister Francisco Pinto Balsemao to aid given to rival Radiotelevisao Portuguesa (RTP).

After going over RTP's books, it said state financing compensated the channel for its public service obligations, ranging from religious programmes to coverage of Madeira and the Azores and cooperation with Portuguese-speaking countries in Africa.

But the Commission is still investigating the complaints lodged by France's TF1, a subsidiary of building giant Bouygues, against France 2 and France 3; Gestevision Telecinco of Spain against RTVE and Spanish regional televisions; and against RAI in Italy.

Taking the view that the Commission was dragging its feet, the first three complainants took their cases to the European Court of First Instance last year asking it to find that the EU executive had failed in its duty to enforce a level playing field in the sector.
BBC's head of European Affairs Matteo Maggiore defended the need for a protocal.
"We support the protocol very strongly. We think there is a problem with the way current EU law approaches the issue of funding in the broadcasting sector," he told Reuters.
"Public funding...is the effect of political decisions in the member states defining the limits of the public service mission," Maggiore said.
But ACT thinks it simply is not justified to exclude public broadcasters from EU competition rules saying that public service obligations were not particular to the television sector.

"The coexistence of public service and competition is even more clear in other sectors (mail, energy, telecommunications, transport etc.) where the European Union institutions have provided, within the framework of the present Treaty, effective solutions to achieve the necessary equilibrium," ACT said in a statement.
In those sectors the EU has been at pains to ensure fair rules for all.

The sources said the Commission does not think that a protocol is appropriate. It is in some degree supported by Britain which would prefer a declaration with less of an effect of exempting the sector from the normal competition rules, one source said.
